summary: Biodiversity and resilience for ages 12–14: define biodiversity at three levels (species, genetic, ecosystem), explain mechanistically why high diversity makes ecosystems more resilient (redundancy and alternative food-web pathways, plus genetic variation as insurance against new stresses), name human threats, and argue that biodiversity loss harms people via ecosystem services. The proposed core activity lets learners apply the SAME shock to a species-rich vs species-poor food web and observe one absorbing it while the other cascades to collapse; a role-play conservation debrief, a reveal-based contrast image, and categorisation/prediction tasks support definition, argument and assessment. High diversity raises the likelihood of absorbing a shock but does not guarantee survival (e.g. loss of a keystone species can still cause collapse). Build throughout on prior food-web/interdependence knowledge.
misconceptions: Thinking biodiversity just means 'lots of animals', missing genetic and ecosystem levels and the variety (not just quantity) of life.
Believing every species is equally dispensable — or, conversely, that only 'important' big species matter — rather than grasping functional redundancy.
Assuming a stable-looking ecosystem is automatically resilient, not realising low diversity can look fine until a shock causes collapse.
Treating biodiversity loss as purely an ethical/animal concern, missing the human dependence on ecosystem services.
Confusing genetic diversity with species diversity, or thinking a large population is automatically genetically diverse.
Thinking one conservation solution is simply 'best', rather than weighing trade-offs among competing solutions.

activities.title: Break two food webs with the same shock
steps: Work with two side-by-side food webs: one high-diversity web with many species and redundant links, and one low-diversity web with few species and single pathways.
Remove the SAME species (or apply the same shock such as a disease or pollutant) to BOTH webs and observe what happens in each.
In the rich web, watch a consumer switch to an alternative prey so the web wobbles and re-stabilises; in the poor web, watch the only pathway sever and a cascade of extinctions ripple outward.

Run a genetic-diversity round: set one population as uniform (clone-like) and one as genetically varied, then unleash a disease; observe survivors remaining in the varied population while the uniform population is highly vulnerable to being wiped out — and note that the real-world outcome is a matter of likelihood, not certainty.
Describe in your own words why the two webs responded differently to the identical shock.
activities.insight: High biodiversity provides redundancy — spare pathways that absorb a shock the way many strands of a net hold when one is cut, while a single strand snaps. Diversity is insurance, and the same principle extends to the gene level: variety is what makes survivors far more likely. High diversity raises the chance of absorbing a shock but does not guarantee it.

activities.title: Conservation-biologist challenge: justify and choose
steps: Take part in a role-play interview where a conservation biologist presses you to justify your reasoning: 'Why would losing one "unimportant" beetle matter?'
Respond to 'We can't save everything — how would you choose?' by weighing trade-offs between competing conservation solutions rather than naming one as simply 'best'.
Connect your argument to ecosystem services, explaining how protecting diversity protects crops, clean water and medicines people depend on.
State explicitly whether biodiversity loss matters to humans or only to wildlife, and give a concrete example.
activities.insight: Why biodiversity matters is both ethical and self-interested: diversity underpins ecosystem services humans rely on, and maintaining it means evaluating and weighing competing solutions, not picking one obvious answer.

activities.title: Reveal and compare: diverse vs degraded, and the services map
steps: Explore a split scene showing a rich reef or meadow beside a degraded version; tap individual species to reveal their roles and how links are redundant or missing.
Use a second layer that pins ecosystem services (pollination, clean water, medicine, soil fertility) to the organisms or habitats that provide them.
Sort examples into the three levels of biodiversity: species diversity (how many different species), genetic diversity (variation within a species), and ecosystem diversity (variety of habitats).
activities.insight: Biodiversity is variety at three distinct levels, not just a headcount of animals, and the human payoff from that variety can be traced to specific services.

activities.title: Classify, predict and match (check and diagnose)
steps: Categorise worked examples into species, genetic, or ecosystem diversity.
Predict which of two webs resists collapse under a shock and state WHY, not just which one.
Match human activities (habitat destruction, pollution, invasive species, climate change, overexploitation) to the biodiversity threat each causes.

Answer the diagnostic: Two grassland fields both have plenty of grazing insects. Field A has 20 different insect species; Field B has just one species, but lots of it. A new disease arrives that kills off one insect species. In Field A it is one of the 20 species; in Field B it is the only species present. Which field's ecosystem is more likely to keep working, and why?
activities.insight: Learners can distinguish the three levels, attribute threats to human drivers, and — crucially — explain resilience by the redundancy/backup mechanism rather than by headcount.

checkQuestion: Two grassland fields both have plenty of grazing insects. Field A has 20 different insect species; Field B has just one species, but lots of it. A new disease arrives that kills off one insect species. Which field's ecosystem is more likely to keep working, and why?
checkAnswer: Field A. With many species, if the disease wipes one out, other species can still do its jobs — pollinating, feeding the birds — so the food web keeps functioning. Field B could collapse because its single species has no backup. High biodiversity gives an ecosystem functional redundancy, so it can absorb a loss and stay stable.
